messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Vignette:
Rangi Taufa is a 63-year-old Tongan-American man who works as a community organizer in a mid-sized Pacific Islander enclave on the West Coast. He came to the clinic after what he described, with some difficulty, as "not being able to keep going the way I have been." He is divorced and lives alone, and the quietness of his apartment, he noted during intake, is something he both needs and finds oppressive.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Rangi was involved in a serious road accident during a community outreach event. He had been driving a van transporting several elderly members of his congregation to a health fair when a commercial truck ran a red light and struck the passenger side at high speed. Emergency responders arrived quickly, and in the chaos that followed, uniformed police officers and paramedics surrounded the vehicle, issuing rapid commands and physically pulling people from the wreckage. Rangi, though injured himself, had been conscious throughout. He remembered with excruciating clarity the sound of metal compressing, the smell of something burning, and the face of one elderly woman as she was lifted past him — and then almost nothing for a period he estimates as perhaps twenty minutes. Those minutes are simply gone. He has no access to them regardless of how hard he tries to recover them, and what surrounds that gap on either side remains fragmentary and inconsistent. He can describe the impact. He cannot describe what happened to the people in his care during the time that matters most to him.

In the weeks after the accident, Rangi found himself returning compulsively to questions of responsibility. He had been the driver. He had chosen that route. He had, he became increasingly certain, made a decision in the seconds before impact — he could not remember what it was, but he was sure it had been wrong. This conviction settled into him quietly and deeply, the way water finds the lowest point in a room. He did not speak of it to anyone.

What he noticed instead, and what confused him, was that his body seemed to have its own understanding of the event that had nothing to do with his conscious reasoning. He would be sitting in a city council meeting, perfectly safe, and his heart would be slamming against his ribs as though he were still in the van. He found this frightening and humiliating in equal measure — he had come to feel that his body was no longer his, that it had turned into something unreliable, something that responded to the world on its own terms without consulting him.

The triggers that came to govern his days were specific and, to him, bewildering in their ordinariness. Police officers at community events — a routine presence in his work — became nearly unbearable. The sight of a uniform, even at a distance, produced a physical response he could neither explain nor suppress, and he began routing his movements through spaces where he was unlikely to encounter them. More disruptive still was his reaction to anger. In his role as a community organizer, conflict is a professional constant — raised voices at meetings, tense negotiations with city officials, a resident's frustrated outburst. Even measured expressions of displeasure from a colleague or a community member were enough to send him somewhere he could not name and could not describe. He had begun canceling meetings, delegating facilitation to junior staff, and withdrawing from the coalition work that had defined his professional life for two decades. Colleagues noticed. He was asked, gently, whether he was all right. He said he was tired.

What he told the intake clinician, haltingly and with long pauses, was that he had stopped feeling like himself some time ago. He used the phrase "dead inside" without apparent distress, as though reporting a fact about the weather. He said he did not know how to talk about what had happened — not because it was too painful, but because the words genuinely did not come. He sat with that for a moment and then said that what had finally brought him in was the recognition that he was disappearing from his own community, and that he did not want to finish his life that way.
